Game theory

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Mathematical optimization
OurBigBook.com Words: 22k Articles: 336
Game theory studies decisions whose consequences depend on what other decision makers choose. A bidder's gain depends on competing bids in an auction; a driver's travel time depends on other drivers in a congestion game. This strategic interdependence makes choosing well a different problem from optimization against a fixed environment: each participant's best response depends on the others' choices.
A normal-form game specifies the players, their available pure strategies, and their payoffs for each strategy profile. Larger payoffs mean more preferred outcomes for that player. Unless stated otherwise, a two-player table below lists (u1​,u2​): the row player's payoff first, the column player's second. Each player maximizes their own expected utility; the numbers need not represent money, and comparing different players' numerical scales is unnecessary.
The central question is whether everyone's choices fit together. A Nash equilibrium consists of mutual best responses: no unilateral deviation improves a player's expected payoff. It can involve definite choices, or mixed strategies that deliberately randomize. Matching pennies shows why randomization can be essential; the coordination game shows how players can share an interest in coordinating while disagreeing over which outcome to choose. Such shared gains are absent from a two-player zero-sum game, where one player's gain is exactly the other's loss.
These ideas are useful both for analyzing incentives and for designing them. Mechanism design asks how changing the rules changes participants' best responses; evolutionary game theory studies how successful strategies spread. The mathematical appeal is that local comparisons of payoffs can reveal a globally consistent pattern of choices. Consistency alone does not imply Pareto efficiency, uniqueness, or that actual play will converge to a Nash equilibrium.
John Nash's [ref] established existence of a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium for every finite game. His [ref] developed the theory beyond two-player zero-sum games. The distinction between conflicting and shared interests is fundamental to the subject.

Algorithmic game theory

Game theory OurBigBook.com

General-sum game

Words: 36
Game theory OurBigBook.com
A game whose players' utilities are specified separately, without assuming a fixed sum. Improving one player's utility need not worsen another's. A finite perfect-information game can be solved by backward induction using entire utility tuples and each moving player's own coordinate, as in max-n search.

Reachability game

Words: 101
Game theory OurBigBook.com
A turn-based game on a directed graph in which a player tries to force a designated target set. Its winning region is a least fixed point: add that player's vertices with some winning successor and the opponent's vertices with all successors winning. The finite-graph version uses the same construction as a winning-position attractor in an infinite game.
With disjoint terminal wins for two players and infinite plays valued as draws, compute both reachability attractors while keeping terminals fixed. Entry ranks give terminating winning strategies; positions outside both regions admit defence avoiding a forced loss. A cycle alone is not a certificate of a draw if it also offers a forceable winning exit.

Absent-minded decision problem

Words: 99
Game theory OurBigBook.com
A decision problem in which the same information set can be reached more than once along a single path, so the decision-maker does not know which visit is occurring. It violates perfect recall. A behavioural strategy uses a common probability at each visit and independent random draws, making terminal probabilities nonlinear in that probability.
For instance, let stopping at the first visit pay zero, continuing and then stopping pay eight, and continuing twice pay one. With continuation probability p, expected payoff is 8p(1−p)+p2=16/7−7(p−4/7)2. Its maximum 16/7 exceeds the best deterministic-plan payoff of one. Randomizing once between the deterministic plans cannot reproduce the two fresh decisions.

Behavioural strategy

Words: 191 Articles: 1
Game theory OurBigBook.com
An assignment of an action probability distribution to every information set of a player in an extensive-form game. Randomization is fresh at each encounter. It differs from a mixed strategy, which chooses a complete deterministic plan once before play. Perfect recall is central to equivalence of their induced outcome distributions.

Mixed and behavioural security levels without perfect recall (vbehavioural​=1/4,vmixed​=1/2)

Words: 149
Behavioural strategy OurBigBook.com
Consider a zero-sum game in which a player chooses a binary action, forgets it, and chooses again, while an opponent makes one hidden binary choice. The first player's payoff is one if all three choices agree and zero otherwise. The later information set merges both initial-action histories. This violates perfect recall without revisiting the same information set, unlike an absent-minded decision problem.
A behavioural strategy chooses the first and second actions with independent left probabilities p,r. Its security level payoff is min(pr,(1−p)(1−r)), since the opponent selects the less favorable target action. This minimum is at most p(1−p)r(1−r)​≤1/4, attained at p=r=1/2.
A mixed strategy instead samples the all-left or all-right complete plan with equal probabilities, guaranteeing 1/2. Against an opponent who chooses each target equally often, each complete constant plan earns 1/2 and each nonconstant plan earns zero, so no mixed strategy can guarantee more. The separation comes from correlation between a sampled plan's actions; fresh independent randomizations cannot retain it after the initial action is forgotten.

Perfect recall

Words: 166 Articles: 1
Game theory OurBigBook.com
A player has perfect recall when the information sets never erase that player's previously available information or earlier chosen actions. With perfect recall, randomizing once over complete pure strategies and using suitable independent randomizations at information sets can induce the same outcome distributions.
Without perfect recall, one information set may be encountered twice on the same play path. A behavioural strategy then uses the same probabilities with fresh draws at both encounters; its outcome distribution need not be attainable by any mixed strategy over deterministic plans.

Kuhn's theorem

Words: 90
Perfect recall OurBigBook.com
In a finite extensive-form game with perfect recall, each mixed strategy has a realization-equivalent behavioural strategy, and every behavioural strategy has a realization-equivalent mixed strategy. The latter direction samples all contingent actions independently in advance. For the former, condition the random complete plan on the player's own action and information history leading to an information set; perfect recall makes that own history common to its nodes. Conditional action probabilities then reproduce the terminal path factors. At an information set reached with zero probability under that player's own plan distribution, choose any action distribution. The result does not assert equivalence without perfect recall.[ref]

Perfect-information game

Words: 31
Game theory OurBigBook.com
An extensive-form game in which each information set contains a single decision node. Each acting player knows the entire preceding sequence of moves. Finite games with this property can be solved for a subgame perfect equilibrium by backward induction.

Information set

Words: 106 Articles: 1
Game theory OurBigBook.com
A collection of decision nodes that the acting player cannot distinguish when choosing an action in an extensive-form game. All nodes in an information set have the same acting player and available actions. A behavioural strategy assigns the same action probabilities throughout that set.

Imperfect information

Words: 67
Information set OurBigBook.com
In an extensive-form game, a player has imperfect information when some decision information set contains more than one node. The player cannot distinguish those histories at the time of acting. This does not itself imply failure of perfect recall: a player can remember all their own earlier information and actions while never having observed an opponent's hidden choice. Conversely, merging histories in which the player's own earlier actions differ violates perfect recall.

Extensive-form game

Words: 625 Articles: 6
Game theory OurBigBook.com
A game described by a game tree, with the acting player and available actions specified at each decision node, payoffs at terminal nodes, and information sets indicating which decision nodes a player can distinguish. A pure strategy specifies an action at every information set belonging to that player, including ones not reached during realized play.

Finite-horizon alternating-offer bargaining

Words: 338 Articles: 2
Extensive-form game OurBigBook.com
Two players alternate proposals for dividing a pie, with a fixed final round. Agreement ends the game; rejection shrinks the next available pie by a factor 0<α<1. Final rejection gives both players zero. Offers range continuously over the entire available pie. Backward induction in games determines immediate agreement and the proposer's share through the continuous-offer bargaining acceptance lemma and the finite-horizon bargaining parity effect. Discrete offer grids can change both the boundary behavior and the exact shares.

Finite-horizon bargaining parity effect (Pk​=1+α1−(−α)k​)

Words: 108
Finite-horizon alternating-offer bargaining OurBigBook.com
In finite-horizon alternating-offer bargaining, the proposer with k rounds left retains fraction Pk​ of the currently available pie. Terminal acceptance gives P1​=1. After rejection, the responder becomes proposer and can obtain fraction αPk−1​ of the current pie. The continuous-offer bargaining acceptance lemma therefore gives Pk​=1−αPk−1​. Summing the resulting finite geometric series proves the displayed formula.
Odd horizons give shares above 1/(1+α), decreasing toward it; even horizons give shares below it, increasing toward it. Between two available horizons k1​<k2​, choose k1​ if k1​ is odd and k2​ if k1​ is even. This concerns the initial proposer and immediate agreement, rather than waiting until the selected final round to obtain its share.

Continuous-offer bargaining acceptance lemma

Words: 163
Finite-horizon alternating-offer bargaining OurBigBook.com
Let a proposer divide a pie of size M>0 by continuously offering its responder q∈[0,M]. Rejection gives fixed continuation payoffs b to the proposer and c to the responder, with 0≤c<M and b<M−c. Then a subgame perfect equilibrium must have the responder accept q=c with probability one. The proposer offers exactly c, retaining M−c.
Sequential rationality forces rejection for q<c and acceptance for q>c. If acceptance at c had probability a<1, that offer would give the proposer a(M−c)+(1−a)b<M−c. Every larger offer gives less than M−c and can be improved by a smaller offer still above c; every smaller offer gives b<M−c. The supremum M−c would therefore be unattained. Randomizing offers cannot attain it either: the nonnegative gap from M−c would be strictly positive almost surely and hence have positive expectation. No best response would exist, contradicting equilibrium. Acceptance at c removes this gap and makes q=c the unique optimal proposal. The assumptions c<M and b<M−c exclude degenerate indifference of the proposer.

Backward induction in games

Words: 194 Articles: 1
Extensive-form game OurBigBook.com
In a finite perfect-information game without chance moves, solve terminal decision points first. At each earlier decision point, its player chooses an action maximizing its own payoff among the already solved continuations. Record a choice in every subgame, including those not reached by the root choice. This constructs a subgame perfect equilibrium. Tied choices may yield several equilibrium strategies and several outcomes. The name refers to Ernst Zermelo; the computational procedure is an application of backward induction.

Unique outcome under strict outcome preferences

Words: 124
Backward induction in games OurBigBook.com
Suppose a finite perfect-information game has no chance moves, and every player strictly ranks the possible outcome labels. Different terminal histories may have the same outcome label and thus the same payoff. Every subgame then has a unique subgame perfect equilibrium outcome, even though its equilibrium strategy need not be unique.
The proof is backward induction. Each child subgame has a unique continuation outcome. The moving player's strict ranking selects exactly one best label among those outcomes. Several actions can tie only by leading to that same label, which proves uniqueness at the current node. For a sequential election, the labels may be winning candidates: a voter can have several optimal ballots, all producing its same favourite achievable winner. If preferences have ties between different labels, the conclusion can fail.

Realization-equivalent strategies

Words: 44
Extensive-form game OurBigBook.com
Two strategies for the same player are realization-equivalent when they induce the same probability distribution on terminal histories against every fixed opposing strategy profile. The requirement is stronger than having equal expected payoff against one particular opponent. For a finite extensive-form game with perfect recall, Kuhn's theorem gives this equivalence between appropriate mixed strategies and behavioural strategies.

Boolean game

Words: 215 Articles: 1
Game theory OurBigBook.com
A finite game represented succinctly by propositional logic. Each player controls a disjoint collection of Boolean variables and chooses their truth values. Together those choices determine a Boolean valuation. A player's goal is a propositional formula, with payoff one if satisfied and zero otherwise. The control sets normally form a set partition of all variables.
A pure strategy strategy profile is a Nash equilibrium if every unsatisfied player remains unsatisfied after every change to that player's controlled variables. Checking a candidate can therefore require solving a Boolean satisfiability problem, even though evaluating its current payoffs is easy.

Candidate equilibrium checking in a Boolean game (coNP-complete)

Words: 135
Boolean game OurBigBook.com
Given a succinct Boolean game and a complete pure strategy strategy profile, determine whether it is a Nash equilibrium. The problem is co-NP-complete for goal propositional formulas, even with one player. This differs from existential equilibrium checking in a Boolean game, which searches for some qualifying Nash equilibrium.
A negative instance has a short complexity certificate: a currently unsatisfied player and new truth values for that player's controlled Boolean variables that make the goal true. Evaluating the current and changed propositional formulas takes polynomial time, proving membership in co-NP.
For hardness, given a propositional formula F(X), let one player control X and a fresh variable z, with goal z∧F(X). The all-false candidate has payoff zero. It is a Nash equilibrium exactly when F is an unsatisfiable Boolean formula, since any satisfying assignment permits an improvement by also setting z true. This is a polynomial-time many-one reduction from unsatisfiability. The fresh guard ensures that the candidate loses independently of the input formula's value there.

Sprague-Grundy theory studies finite acyclic impartial games under the normal-play convention by assigning each position a Grundy number. The assignment recursively takes the minimum excludant of the values of all legal followers. The Sprague-Grundy theorem then reduces a disjunctive sum of games to the bitwise exclusive or of its component values. Prisoner's dilemma (T>R>P>S)

Words: 1k Articles: 12
Game theory OurBigBook.com
Two people can each have a clear incentive to choose an outcome that leaves both worse off. The prisoner's dilemma isolates this tension between individual best responses and Pareto efficiency. For example, two partners can each save effort by withholding a promised contribution, yet both would prefer a successful joint project to mutual withholding. The model applies when each person's payoffs really have the ordering below; the names “cooperate” and “defect” alone do not establish a prisoner's dilemma.
In the symmetric two-player normal-form game, each player chooses cooperation C or defection D simultaneously, without observing the other's current choice. The four payoffs are the mutual-cooperation reward R, mutual-defection punishment P, sole-defector temptation T, and sole-cooperator payoff S, with T>R>P>S. Defection is a strictly dominant strategy: it beats cooperation against either opposing pure strategy. This definition and the resulting one-shot Nash equilibrium are discussed in Steven Kuhn, Prisoner's Dilemma, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, section 1.
Take the concrete payoffs T=5, R=3, P=1, S=0. Each entry below gives the row player's payoff followed by the column player's payoff:
CD​C(3,3)(5,0)​D(0,5)(1,1)​​
(2)
For the row player, switching from C to D improves the payoff from 3 to 5 against C, and from 0 to 1 against D. The column player has the same comparisons, so D is a strictly dominant strategy for each. Even against a mixed strategy choosing C with probability q, the expected payoff advantage is 2q+(1−q)=1+q>0. Thus cooperation cannot appear with positive probability in a best response, and (D,D) is the unique one-shot Nash equilibrium, including mixed strategies.
At (D,D), a unilateral deviation to C lowers the deviator's payoff from 1 to 0. A joint change to (C,C) instead raises both payoffs from 1 to 3: mutual cooperation Pareto dominates mutual defection, making the Nash equilibrium fail Pareto efficiency. A Nash equilibrium tests unilateral deviations, so it need not maximize shared gains. This is the useful lesson: improving the available outcome may require changing incentives, rather than telling each participant to choose a better best response.
The additional inequality 2R≥T+S says that mutual cooperation gives each player at least as much average payoff as equal-time alternation between the two asymmetric outcomes. It is a further assumption, not a consequence of T>R>P>S. Here it holds strictly: 6>5, and alternating exploitation gives each player average payoff 5/2<3. This comparison concerns equal-time averages, not every discounted sequence. See Kuhn, section 3, on the additional cardinal-payoff condition.

Iterated prisoner's dilemma

Words: 1k Articles: 10
Prisoner's dilemma OurBigBook.com
The iterated prisoner's dilemma is a repeated game with a prisoner's dilemma at each round. Earlier choices can change later best responses: a present gain from defection may be outweighed by lost future cooperation. A pure strategy now specifies an action after every possible observed history, including histories that its own prescribed play would never reach. The horizon, observations, initial actions, and payoff convention must be specified before assessing a Nash equilibrium or subgame perfect equilibrium.
For the following worked example, repeat the prisoner's dilemma above infinitely at rounds t=0,1,…. Assume public perfect monitoring: after each round both players observe both actions exactly, without error. They share a discount factor 0≤δ<1 and evaluate a path of stage payoffs ui​(t) using the normalized discounted payoff
Ui​=(1−δ)∑t=0∞​δtui​(t).
(3)
The round-zero weight is one before normalization, including when δ=0. A larger discount factor gives future payoffs more weight; the geometric series makes a constant stage payoff have the same normalized value. These assumptions and normalization follow [ref]. The numerical payoffs here are our 3,5,0,1 example; the lecture uses a different table.
Suppose both players use grim trigger: play C initially and while every past action of both players was C; after any observed D, play D forever. With no unilateral deviation, each gets normalized payoff 3. A first unilateral deviation to D earns 5 now, then at most 1 each round because the opponent switches permanently to always defect. The deviator attains that continuation payoff by choosing D thereafter. At any history of mutual cooperation, the comparison is therefore
Ucooperate​=3,Udeviate​=(1−δ)5+δ⋅1=5−4δ.
(4)
Cooperation is a best response precisely when
3≥5−4δ⟺δ≥21​.
(5)
Equivalently, without normalization the geometric series gives
Vcooperate​=1−δ3​,Vdeviate​=5+1−δδ​.
(6)
Multiplying both unnormalized payoffs by the same positive factor 1−δ leaves the best response comparison unchanged.
For example, with discount factor δ=1/4, the first unilateral deviation gives normalized payoff 4>3, so mutual grim trigger is not a Nash equilibrium. At δ=3/4, it gives 2<3, so cooperation is preferable. At δ=1/2 the two payoffs tie: the incentive to cooperate is weak, which is sufficient for a subgame perfect equilibrium.
The punishment is credible after every history containing a defection: the opponent's pure strategy then prescribes D forever, and D remains the stage best response, earning 1 rather than 0. Together with the cooperative-history comparison, this establishes mutual grim trigger as a subgame perfect equilibrium for 1/2≤δ<1. Delaying the first unilateral deviation merely delays the same gain or loss; further cooperation during punishment only lowers the deviator's payoff. Mutual always defect also remains a subgame perfect equilibrium, so patience permits cooperation without making it inevitable.
This calculation assumes an infinite horizon and δ<1; it does not define a discounted payoff at δ=1. With a finite, commonly known final round and positive weight on each round, backward induction instead gives mutual defection in every round of this stage game. Observational errors change the model too: one mistaken defection permanently activates grim trigger. Historical dependence, initial memories, and the payoff time convention also affect whether a cooperative rule resists or invades other pure strategies; the existing reactive strategy and Tit for tat discussions concern those additional questions.

A grim trigger is a history-dependent pure strategy in a repeated game that switches permanently to punishment after a trigger event. In the iterated prisoner's dilemma above, the trigger is any player's observed defection, and punishment is always defect. Unlike Tit for tat, grim trigger never restores cooperation after the opponent cooperates again. Whether mutual grim trigger is a subgame perfect equilibrium depends on the stage payoffs, discount factor, and monitoring assumptions; it is not an unconditional property of the rule. See Ozdaglar, lecture 15, slides 12–15.

Evolutionary game theory

Words: 2k Articles: 4
Game theory OurBigBook.com
Evolutionary game theory studies how a population's composition changes when the success of a pure strategy depends on which other pure strategies it encounters. The central feedback is a frequency-dependent payoff: becoming common changes the opponents a strategy meets, which can change whether it does well. In a coordination game, common behaviour can reinforce itself; in the coexistence example below, being rare is an advantage. This makes evolutionary game theory useful for asking which behaviours can persist and which initial compositions lead to different outcomes, without assuming that each participant solves an optimization problem.
In the basic model, a large, well-mixed population has finitely many inherited pure strategies; interactions sample opponents according to their population frequencies. Assume that a strategy's expected payoff determines its per capita net reproductive growth rate, with a common baseline allowed. These are modelling assumptions: reproduction must transmit the strategy, encounters must match the proposed sampling rule, and the conversion from payoff to growth must be justified for an application. The replicator equation below describes the resulting continuous-time frequencies. Taylor and Jonker's [ref] explicitly derive this growth model.
For learned behaviour, reproduction can instead be replaced by an assumed copying rule: an individual samples another individual uniformly and copies a better-performing pure strategy at a rate proportional to the positive payoff difference. At frequencies xi​,xj​, the net flow from j to i is xi​xj​(fi​−fj​), because the two directional positive parts subtract to fi​−fj​. Summing over j gives xi​(fi​−fˉ​), the replicator equation. This derivation states a particular mechanism; an arbitrary rule for learning or imitation need not give the same dynamical system.
Three questions must be distinguished. A symmetric Nash equilibrium tests whether an individual can improve its expected payoff against the resident composition. An evolutionarily stable strategy tests whether each distinct rare mutant is outperformed after it is introduced. Dynamical stability tests the response of an actual dynamical system to small changes of composition, and asymptotic stability additionally requires nearby trajectories to converge. For a finite symmetric bimatrix game under the continuous-time replicator equation, every evolutionarily stable strategy is a symmetric Nash equilibrium and a locally asymptotically stable rest point; the converse from asymptotic stability to an evolutionarily stable strategy fails in general. See Ross Cressman and Yi Tao, The replicator equation and other game dynamics (2014), Theorems 1–2 and Example 1. These statements refer to stability on the full probability simplex, including perturbations introducing currently absent pure strategies.
A concrete experiment makes the frequency feedback visible. In 2009, Gore, Youk and van Oudenaarden competed two yeast strains: a producer of the enzyme invertase, which enables sucrose hydrolysis, and a mutant lacking the corresponding SUC2 gene. Released sugars can feed neighbours, so avoiding production can be advantageous. They used shaken 5 mL cultures with 5% sucrose at 30∘C, diluted daily after 23 hours of growth. Different labelled proteins allowed the two strains to be counted separately by flow cytometry; selective plating periodically checked the counts. The cooperator required externally supplied histidine, so restricting that amino acid imposed an adjustable growth disadvantage. See Snowdrift game dynamics and facultative cheating in yeast, pp. 253 and 255–256, Methods Summary.
Starting with rare producers and, separately, rare nonproducers tested both invasion directions. Under the reported coexistence conditions each rare strain increased; changing histidine or added glucose shifted the eventual composition. Their explanation used nonlinear growth benefits, rather than a fixed pairwise payoff matrix. This motivates testing both rarity regimes before inferring an evolutionarily stable strategy or fitting a replicator equation; it does not identify the illustrative tables below with measured payoffs. See Gore, Youk and van Oudenaarden, Figures 1–3.
An early motivation was understanding why animal contests can involve restraint even when escalation might win an individual encounter. Maynard Smith and Price's [ref] introduced the evolutionarily stable strategy in this setting. Taylor and Jonker's [ref] then studied explicit continuous and discrete dynamics. Static resistance to invasion and the paths populations follow are related questions, but they require separate definitions.

The replicator equation says that a strategy grows in frequency when its expected payoff exceeds the population's current mean payoff. It is an ordinary differential equation for a composition, rather than for total population size. The subtraction of the mean is what makes relative success matter: even a type growing in absolute number can shrink as a fraction if other types grow faster.
Let xi​(t) be the frequency of pure strategy i, with n available pure strategies and
x∈Δn​={x∈Rn:xi​≥0, ∑i=1n​xi​=1}.
(8)
In a symmetric bimatrix game, let the payoff matrix A have entry aij​ equal to the payoff to strategy i against j. The other player's payoff in that encounter is aji​: symmetry between player roles does not require A=AT. Uniform random encounters give the expected payoffs and their population mean
fi​(x)=(Ax)i​=∑j​aij​xj​,fˉ​(x)=∑i​xi​fi​(x)=xTAx.
(9)
After choosing the time unit so that the growth-rate scale is one, the continuous-time replicator equation is
x˙i​=xi​(fi​(x)−fˉ​(x))=xi​((Ax)i​−xTAx),i=1,…,n.
(10)
Here a payoff is measured on a scale proportional to net growth per unit time, not merely as an arbitrary preference ranking. More generally one can specify locally Lipschitz frequency-dependent payoffs fi​(x) directly; the same equation with fˉ​=∑i​xi​fi​ then defines a unique frequency trajectory. The linear pairwise model and its reproductive interpretation are given in Taylor and Jonker (1978), sections 2–3; the formulas here also follow by the following direct normalization.
Suppose the number Ni​ of type i obeys N˙i​=Ni​[b(t)+fi​(x)], where the baseline b(t) is identical for all types. Set N=∑i​Ni​>0 and xi​=Ni​/N. The quotient rule gives
N˙=N[b(t)+fˉ​(x)],x˙i​=N2N˙i​N−Ni​N˙​=xi​(fi​−fˉ​).
(11)
Thus the common baseline cancels. Adding the same constant to every entry of A leaves the replicator equation unchanged; multiplying A by a positive constant changes only the speed along trajectories. The same payoff matrix can therefore describe frequency evolution at different growth-rate baselines and time scales.
The probability simplex is invariant in forward time. On ∑i​xi​=1,
∑i​x˙i​=∑i​xi​fi​−fˉ​∑i​xi​=0.

xi​(t)=xi​(0)exp(∫0t​[fi​(x(s))−fˉ​(x(s))]ds).
(13)
An absent type remains absent, and a positive frequency remains positive at every finite time. For the fixed payoff matrix model, bounded rates on the compact probability simplex give global forward solutions. Frequencies can still tend to zero as t→∞. Each face is invariant, so this model has no spontaneous introduction of new pure strategies; mutation or outside introductions would require additional terms. For two present types the logarithm of their frequency ratio satisfies dtd​log(xi​/xj​)=fi​−fj​, directly expressing the accumulated payoff advantage.
For two pure strategies, write the composition as (x,1−x), where x is the frequency of strategy 1, and let
A=(ac​bd​),f1​=ax+b(1−x),f2​=cx+d(1−x).
(14)
Their payoff difference and the resulting scalar ordinary differential equation are
Δf(x)=f1​−f2​=(b−d)+(a−b−c+d)x,x˙=F(x)=x(1−x)Δf(x).
(15)
In the interior 0<x<1, the sign of the payoff difference determines the direction of motion. The endpoints are always equilibrium points, and an additional interior equilibrium point exists precisely when the affine payoff difference has a zero strictly between them. At a simple interior zero x∗​, F′(x∗​)=x∗​(1−x∗​)Δf′(x∗​): a negative value gives asymptotic stability, a positive value gives instability. At the endpoints F′(0)=b−d and F′(1)=c−a, with stability understood relative to [0,1]. A zero derivative requires examining the actual flow rather than this strict sign test.
For an original coordination game, imagine two conventions that reward matching, with convention 1 giving the larger matching reward. Choose
Acoord​=(30​02​),f1​=3x,f2​=2(1−x),x˙=x(1−x)(5x−2).
(16)
The crossing is x∗​=2/5. Below it, convention 1 loses frequency; above it, convention 1 gains frequency. The endpoint equilibrium points 0 and 1 have one-sided asymptotic stability, while 2/5 is unstable: the corresponding derivatives are −2,−3 and 6/5, respectively. Every initial 0<x(0)<2/5 tends to 0, every initial 2/5<x(0)<1 tends to 1, and exactly x(0)=2/5 stays there. Even the convention with the larger matching reward can disappear if it starts below the threshold. This is bistability, not selection of a universally best convention.
The compositions giving a symmetric Nash equilibrium in this coordination game are the two pure conventions and the mixed composition (2/5,3/5). Both pure conventions are evolutionarily stable strategies because a mutant convention has strictly lower payoff against the pure resident. The mixed symmetric Nash equilibrium is not an evolutionarily stable strategy: against that resident both conventions tie, but after a pure convention-1 mutant is introduced its payoff advantage is 5(x−2/5)>0. Equal payoffs at a symmetric Nash equilibrium need not provide resistance to invasion or asymptotic stability.
For an original coexistence model, choose payoffs making each convention advantageous when sufficiently rare:
Acoex​=(12​30​),f1​=3−2x,f2​=2x,x˙=x(1−x)(3−4x).
(17)
Here x∗​=3/4 attracts every initial composition with both types present: x˙>0 below it and x˙<0 above it. The interior derivative is F′(3/4)=−3/4, while F′(0)=3 and F′(1)=1 make both endpoints unstable to introduction of the other type. The endpoints nevertheless remain stationary if the other type is exactly absent; the attraction statement excludes those boundary initial states.
The sole symmetric Nash equilibrium in this coexistence model is p=(3/4,1/4). It is also an evolutionarily stable strategy. For any different mixed strategy q=(y,1−y), the first comparison in the two-condition criterion for evolutionary stability ties because Ap=(3/2,3/2). Its second comparison is strictly positive:
pTAq−qTAq=(p−q)TAq=(3/4−y)(3−4y)=4(y−3/4)2>0.
(18)
Thus restoring frequency feedback can protect a mixture even though all present types earn equal payoffs at the mixture. Coexistence here means different individuals using different pure strategies; it does not require every individual to randomize with a mixed strategy.
Frequency evolution need not increase the mean payoff. In the coexistence example fˉ​=5x−4x2, whose maximum occurs at x=5/8, whereas the attracting composition is 3/4. For 5/8<x<3/4, the frequency x increases while dtd​fˉ​=(5−8x)x˙<0. Individual payoff advantages drive the equation; maximizing collective mean payoff is a different optimization problem.
More generally, a rest point only equalizes payoffs among present types: xi​>0 implies (Ax)i​=xTAx. A symmetric Nash equilibrium additionally requires (Ax)i​≤xTAx for every absent type. All vertices are rest points even when an absent type could invade. For finite symmetric bimatrix games, a rest point with Lyapunov stability on the full probability simplex is a symmetric Nash equilibrium; an interior trajectory that converges has a symmetric Nash equilibrium as its limit. These are conditional results, not a convergence theorem for every trajectory. See Cressman and Tao (2014), Theorem 1.
The rock paper scissors payoff matrix gives an explicit obstruction to universal convergence:
A=​01−1​−101​1−10​​.
(19)
Since AT=−A, xTAx=0, and in the interior dtd​log(x1​x2​x3​)=∑i​(Ax)i​=0. Thus x1​x2​x3​ is conserved. Its maximum on the probability simplex occurs only at (1/3,1/3,1/3), the unique symmetric Nash equilibrium, so an interior trajectory starting elsewhere cannot converge to that composition. Every other interior product level is a closed curve without a rest point, giving a periodic orbit. The existence of these cycles is also discussed in Cressman and Tao (2014), Example 1. The useful lesson is to inspect the specified payoff feedback and dynamical system, rather than infer convergence from the existence of an evolutionarily stable strategy or a Nash equilibrium.

Frequency-dependent payoff (fi​(x))

Words: 54
Evolutionary game theory OurBigBook.com
A frequency-dependent payoff is an expected payoff depending on the population composition x. Under random pairwise encounters with a fixed payoff matrix it is the linear function fi​(x)=(Ax)i​. The relative advantage fi​(x)−fj​(x) can change sign as opponents become more or less common. The replicator equation converts this feedback into changes of frequency; nonlinear frequency-dependent payoffs allow interactions not represented by a fixed pairwise table.

Repeated game

Words: 454 Articles: 7
Game theory OurBigBook.com
A repeated game plays a stage game over several rounds, allowing actions to depend on earlier observations. Its payoff convention must specify a finite horizon, a discount factor or a long-time average; these need not have identical invasion properties.

Finite-state strategy

Words: 66
Repeated game OurBigBook.com
A history-dependent pure strategy represented by a finite-state machine with an initial automaton state, an action output for each state, and an automaton transition after each observed completed joint action. A grim trigger strategy uses a following state and an absorbing punishment state. Two such deterministic machines jointly form a finite deterministic state system, so their action path is eventually periodic. Its long-run average payoffs are the averages over the eventual cycle; a finite initial prefix has vanishing weight.

Stage game

Words: 36
Repeated game OurBigBook.com
The normal-form game played once in each round of a repeated game. Its actions and payoffs are distinct from the repeated interaction's history-dependent pure strategies and aggregate payoffs. The same stage game can produce different incentive constraints under a finite sum, discounting or long-run average payoff criterion.

Folk theorem for repeated games

Words: 118
Repeated game OurBigBook.com
A family of results describing the large set of Nash equilibrium payoffs available in indefinitely repeated interaction. For a finite game with observed past play, the discounted Nash version supports any feasible, strictly individually rational payoff in a repeated game when players are sufficiently patient.[ref]
The mechanism is to prescribe a path and punish the first deviator by holding that player's future payoff to its minmax payoff. With long-run average payoffs, a finite gain disappears from the average; with discounting, the promised future loss must outweigh the gain. Weak boundary points require care when a stated theorem assumes strict inequalities. A construction proving a Nash equilibrium need not prove a subgame perfect equilibrium, because the punishers' continuation incentives may fail.

Individually rational payoff in a repeated game

Words: 51
Repeated game OurBigBook.com
A payoff vector giving every player at least that player's minmax payoff. It is strictly individually rational if every inequality is strict. A player can reject an equilibrium offering less than the guaranteed amount by choosing a securing strategy instead. These bounds concern repeated-game incentives; they are distinct from participation constraints in mechanism design.

Repeated game OurBigBook.com
The lowest expected payoff to which a player's opponents can hold that player when the player chooses a best response. The opponents' permitted randomization and correlation conventions should be specified for games with several opponents. In a two-player finite game, this equals the player's maximum guaranteed expected payoff by the minimax theorem applied to that player's payoff matrix. This equality does not make the original two-player game a zero-sum game.

The convex hull of the stage game's attainable payoff vectors. Public randomization or deterministic sequences with prescribed limiting frequencies produce such average payoffs. It can be larger than the set attainable using independent mixed strategies in a single stage.

A repeated game criterion evaluating the average stage payoff over increasingly long horizons. State how paths without a limit are treated, for example by using a lower limit. Changing a finite prefix does not change a convergent long-run average payoff. Thus a one-time gain can be outweighed by permanent future punishment without specifying a discount factor.

Payoff (ui​(s1​,…,sn​))

Words: 126 Articles: 1
Game theory OurBigBook.com
A payoff is the number assigned to a player's outcome at a strategy profile, with larger numbers preferred. In the usual expected utility model, expected payoffs are probability-weighted averages of these numbers. If a payoff is specified as money and a player has preferences involving risk, first apply the relevant utility function; maximizing expected money assumes risk neutrality. In a two-player zero-sum game, one player's payoff is the negative of the other's. General bimatrix games instead require a payoff matrix for each player.

Payoff OurBigBook.com
For a finite game, let s=(s1​,…,sn​) range over all pure strategy strategy profiles, and let σj​(sj​) be player j's probability of choosing sj​. Under independent mixed strategies, the probability of s is ∏j​σj​(sj​). The displayed sum is the expected value of player i's payoff. Holding everyone else's mixed strategy fixed makes Ui​ a linear function of σi​; this is why checking pure strategy deviations suffices to check all mixed strategy deviations.

Costly turnout game

Game theory OurBigBook.com
Each voter chooses whether to incur a voting cost. The collective result changes each voter's payoff, and abstention can be optimal when other voters are likely to determine the outcome. The payoff difference between voting and abstaining is the benefit of being pivotal, weighted by the pivotal probability, minus the turnout cost.

Costly turnout game OurBigBook.com
Suppose turnout costs 3c>0, each supporter gains 4c on passage, and the opponent loses 8c. The symmetric-supporter Nash equilibria (α,β,γ) are (0,1/4,1/4) and (1,3/4,3/4). Allowing different supporter probabilities adds (1/4,0,3/8) and (1/4,3/8,0). These follow by comparing the pivotal voting probabilities with the turnout cost; no player benefits by changing their mixed strategy.

Pivotal voting probability

Costly turnout game OurBigBook.com
A voter is pivotal when changing only that voter's participation changes the election result. For an opponent facing two independent supporters with participation probabilities β,γ, under a rule requiring strictly more votes in favour, the opponent is pivotal when exactly one supporter votes. This probability is β(1−γ)+(1−β)γ.

Nonatomic congestion game

Words: 88
Game theory OurBigBook.com
In a nonatomic congestion game, a divisible population chooses resources whose costs depend on aggregate usage. Each individual has negligible size, so changing their choice does not alter those costs. For traffic on a flow network, strategies are routes and an equilibrium is a Wardrop equilibrium: every route with positive flow has minimum delay for its source-sink pair. This differs from a finite-player congestion game, where a deviation changes the load used to evaluate the deviator's new cost. Continuous nondecreasing link delays give a Beckmann potential whose minimizers are exactly the traffic equilibria.

Congestion game

Words: 75
Game theory OurBigBook.com
Players select sets of resources, and each resource's cost depends on its total number of users. Each player's cost is the sum of the costs of their selected resources. A unilateral deviation changes resource loads, so a finite-player Nash equilibrium compares costs after that change, not at the old loads. For cost functions ce​, the potential ∑e​∑j=1ne​​ce​(j) changes by exactly the deviator's cost change. A minimizer of this potential in a finite game is therefore a pure Nash equilibrium.

Evolutionarily stable strategy (e(x∗,(1−ϵ)x∗+ϵy)>e(y,(1−ϵ)x∗+ϵy))

Words: 441 Articles: 4
Game theory OurBigBook.com
A resident strategy is evolutionarily stable if every distinct mutant earns lower expected fitness when introduced at sufficiently small positive frequency. The upper bound on the frequency may depend on the mutant. In a finite symmetric matrix game, e(x,y)=xTAy is the expected payoff, with the second argument representing the population strategy. Affineness in this argument yields the two-condition criterion for evolutionary stability. Every evolutionarily stable strategy is a symmetric Nash equilibrium, but a tied best response must also be strictly outperformed against its own mutant population. The Hawk-Dove game supplies an interior stable mixture despite equality of all payoffs against the resident mixture.

Selection gradient (g(x)=∂y​f(y,x)∣y=x​)

Words: 64
Evolutionarily stable strategy OurBigBook.com
For a differentiable rare-mutant invasion fitness f(y,x) against resident trait x, the selection gradient gives the first-order growth advantage of a nearby mutant. A zero gradient is a candidate interior evolutionary singularity. Strict local uninvadability follows from negative mutant-fitness curvature; evolutionary approach additionally requires the gradient to point toward the candidate. Boundary traits require one-sided tests. A gradient alone does not prove global evolutionary stability.

Hawk-Dove game (e(p,q)=V(1−q)/2+p(V−Dq)/2)

Words: 201 Articles: 1
Evolutionarily stable strategy OurBigBook.com
Hawk fights for a resource of value V, while Dove retreats from Hawk and shares with another Dove. Hawk–Hawk competition incurs damage cost D. The expected payoff difference between Hawk probabilities p,r against population probability q is (p−r)(V−Dq)/2. For positive V,D, pure Hawk is an evolutionarily stable strategy when V>D. At V=D, it remains stable because a mutant p<1 loses V(1−p)2/2 against its own population. When 0<V<D, the stable mixture has Hawk probability p∗=V/D: all first-condition payoffs tie, and its second-condition advantage is D(p−p∗)2/2>0. For nonpositive resource values, pure Dove is stable if V<0 or if V=0<D. At V=D=0 all payoffs vanish and there is no evolutionarily stable strategy.

Chicken payoff ordering (T>R>S>P)

Words: 85
Hawk-Dove game OurBigBook.com
The Chicken payoff ordering describes a symmetric two-player bimatrix game in which aggression earns temptation T against yielding, mutual yielding earns R, yielding to aggression earns S, and mutual aggression earns P, with the displayed strict ordering. Aggression is a best response to yielding, and yielding is a best response to aggression. Thus the two asymmetric action pairs are pure strategy Nash equilibria. The Hawk-Dove game has this ordering in its positive-resource regime where the damage cost exceeds the resource value. In the prisoner's dilemma, the ordering of S and P is reversed, making defection a strictly dominant strategy instead.

Two-condition criterion for evolutionary stability (Ay​≥0,Ay​=0⟹By​>0)

Words: 80
Evolutionarily stable strategy OurBigBook.com
For mixed-strategy expected payoffs put Ay​=e(x∗,x∗)−e(y,x∗) and By​=e(x∗,y)−e(y,y). The invasion payoff difference is exactly (1−ϵ)Ay​+ϵBy​. Positivity for all sufficiently small positive ϵ forces Ay​≥0 by taking the limit. When Ay​=0, it forces By​>0. Conversely Ay​>0 makes the difference positive for sufficiently small frequency, and Ay​=0,By​>0 makes it positive for every positive frequency. Apply this separately to every distinct mutant. This proves the equivalence with an evolutionarily stable strategy; affineness in population composition is essential to the formula.

Game theory OurBigBook.com
A player maximizes the worst payoff it can receive against the other player's actions. Allowing the opponent to mix does not lower the worst payoff beyond a pure action, since the payoff is linear in that mixture. A security level payoff is an individual guarantee, not generally a Nash equilibrium payoff.

Nash bargaining problem ((F,d))

Words: 501 Articles: 11
Game theory OurBigBook.com
The essential two-person bargaining domain consists of a compact convex set of feasible utility vectors F, a disagreement point d∈F, and at least one feasible vector strictly exceeding d coordinatewise. The Nash bargaining solution selects a jointly feasible improvement using a rule characterized by Pareto efficiency, bargaining symmetry, positive affine invariance in bargaining and bargaining independence of irrelevant alternatives.

Nash bargaining problem OurBigBook.com
For a compact convex set of feasible payoff vectors F and a specified disagreement point d, the negotiation set is its individually rational Pareto frontier. It is the set of efficient agreements each player prefers at least weakly to disagreement. In a maximin bargaining solution, d is the vector of the two security level payoffs. This usage is distinct from objection-and-counterobjection bargaining sets in coalitional-game theory.

Nash bargaining problem OurBigBook.com
A feasible payoff vector u′ jointly dominates u if every coordinate is at least as large and at least one is strictly larger. A Pareto optimal vector has no feasible joint dominator. Strict increase of every coordinate is not required. This compares each player's own utilities, not the numerical size of utilities across different players.

Nash bargaining problem OurBigBook.com
A payoff is individually rational for a Nash bargaining problem when neither player receives less than its disagreement point payoff. Essentiality permits strict improvement for both. Maximizing a positive Nash product therefore selects a strictly individually rational payoff.

Nash bargaining problem OurBigBook.com
If an admissible smaller feasible set with the same disagreement point contains the original chosen vector, deleting the other outcomes must leave the choice unchanged. The Nash bargaining solution satisfies this axiom because its unique product maximizer remains feasible.

Transforming each utility by an independent positive affine map must transform the chosen payoff by the same map. The Nash product changes only by a positive factor, so the Nash bargaining solution has this invariance.

Bargaining symmetry

Nash bargaining problem OurBigBook.com
When the feasible payoff set and disagreement point are invariant under interchange of players, the solution must give both players the same payoff.

Nash bargaining problem OurBigBook.com
For an essential Nash bargaining problem, maximizing the Nash product gives a unique vector: on positive gains its logarithm is a strictly concave function. The rule satisfies the four bargaining axioms, and the supporting triangle for Nash bargaining proves their converse characterization. The nonessential case requires additional conventions, since a zero product may have many maximizers.

Nash bargaining solution OurBigBook.com
For a finite two-person game, let di​ be player i's security level payoff, obtained by maximizing its minimum expected payoff against the other player's actions. Apply the Nash bargaining solution to the convexified feasible payoff region with this disagreement point. This is the maximin bargaining solution. “Maximin” specifies the disagreement guarantees; the arbitration objective function remains the Nash product, not the minimum of two numerically incomparable utilities.

Nash bargaining solution OurBigBook.com
Normalize a positive Nash product maximizer and the disagreement point to (1,1) and zero. The first-order product inequality along every feasible segment places the transformed set in z1​+z2​≤2. Compactness allows a symmetric containing triangle with finite lower coordinate bounds. Bargaining symmetry and Pareto efficiency choose (1,1) in that triangle; bargaining independence of irrelevant alternatives transfers this choice to the original normalized set. Positive affine invariance in bargaining then proves the full characterization.

The product of the two players' gains over the disagreement point is maximized over the individually rational feasible set in the Nash bargaining solution. The disagreement point specifies each player's payoff if bargaining fails. It supplies the baseline from which the Nash product measures gains. In a game-based example it may be set to the vector of security level payoffs; this choice must be recomputed when the underlying payoff matrices change.

Cooperative game theory

Words: 4k Articles: 60
Game theory OurBigBook.com
Cooperative game theory studies what groups of players can achieve together and how their joint value can be allocated. A transferable utility game assigns a real value to each coalition. The core of a cooperative game asks which allocations no coalition can improve upon; the Shapley value averages marginal contributions across player orderings.

Transferable utility game (v:2N→R,v(∅)=0)

Words: 4k Articles: 59
Cooperative game theory OurBigBook.com
A finite transferable utility game gives each coalition S⊆N a real value v(S) that its members can distribute among themselves. The usual normalization is v(∅)=0. An efficient payoff vector x satisfies ∑i∈N​xi​=v(N). Simple cooperative games model winning coalitions with values zero and one; convex cooperative games model increasing marginal contributions.

Cooperative cost game (p(N)=c(N),p(S)≤c(S))

Words: 328 Articles: 3
Transferable utility game OurBigBook.com
A transferable utility game formulated as costs c(S) to be shared among members of each coalition S, with c(∅)=0. Its cost core consists of payment vectors p satisfying the displayed efficiency and coalition inequalities, where p(S)=∑i∈S​pi​. A coalition should not be charged more than its standalone cost. Changing signs to v=−c and x=−p converts these conditions to the usual benefit-game core of a cooperative game. The Shapley value can be applied directly to costs, giving payments whose sum is c(N).
Airport problem
Words: 227 Articles: 1
Cooperative cost game OurBigBook.com
Share a runway's cost among users needing different runway lengths. If user i needs a facility costing Ci​≥0, a nonempty coalition pays c(S)=maxi∈S​Ci​, and c(∅)=0. This is a subadditive cost game because the maximum of two nonnegative costs does not exceed their sum. A cost-core allocation always exists: charge the whole cost to one longest-runway user and zero to all others. The Shapley value of an airport game gives a symmetric alternative that also lies in the cost core.
Shapley value of an airport game (ϕj​=λ∑i=1j​Ni​si​−si−1​​)
Words: 154
Airport problem OurBigBook.com
Suppose the distinct required runway lengths are 0=s0​<s1​<⋯<sk​, with ni​>0 users of type i, constant cost λ≥0 per unit length, and suffix counts Ni​=∑ℓ=ik​nℓ​. Then every type-j user has the displayed Shapley value. For layer i, exactly Ni​ users require it. The first of them in a uniformly random permutation contributes its entire cost λ(si​−si−1​). Each requiring user has probability 1/Ni​ of being first. Linearity of the Shapley value sums these expected marginal contributions across the layers that user needs.
The allocation lies in the cost core. Its payments sum to the full runway cost. For any coalition S, its total payment toward layer i is λ(si​−si−1​)∣S∩Ri​∣/Ni​, where Ri​ is the set of users requiring that layer. This is zero if S needs no such layer, and at most the full layer cost otherwise. Summing gives ∑j∈S​ϕj​≤c(S). Suffix counts followed by prefix sums compute all distinct type payments in O(k) arithmetic operations.

The probabilistic Banzhaf index averages a player's marginal contribution over all coalitions not containing that player, each given equal weight. In a simple cooperative game, it is the probability of changing a losing coalition into a winning one when every other player joins independently with probability 1/2. Its sum over players need not equal the grand-coalition value: in a three-player majority game each player has index 1/2, giving total 3/2 despite v(N)=1. This convention differs from both the raw count of pivotal coalitions and the normalized Banzhaf index.
The name refers to John Banzhaf, whose 1965 paper addresses the mathematical analysis of weighted voting.[ref]

The terms v(T) and v(T∪{i,j}) cancel on subtraction, leaving the displayed identity. In a weighted voting game with wi​≤wj​, every summand is nonnegative, proving that the index is monotone in the player's weight. Equal weights give equal indices, although different weights can also have equal indices.

The normalized Banzhaf index rescales the probabilistic Banzhaf indices to sum to the grand-coalition value, whenever the denominator is nonzero. It preserves cooperative-game symmetry and assigns zero to a null player, but generally fails cooperative-game additivity. For example, add the three-player majority game to a dictatorship of player one. Their normalized indices are (1/3,1/3,1/3) and (1,0,0), whereas the sum game has normalized index (6/5,2/5,2/5), not their vector sum. The sum game has grand-coalition value two, which must be retained in the normalization.

A transferable utility game represented by a weighted undirected graph, with one player per graph vertex. Write column j of a two-row binary game as ((aj​,cj​),(bj​,dj​))T, with the row player's payoff first. If there is no pure Nash equilibrium, the column player's maximum payoff in each row must be one. Otherwise every column would be a best response in a zero-payoff row, and excluding an equilibrium there would force the opposite row to dominate in every column, giving an equilibrium in that opposite row.
A column maximizing the column player's top-row payoff must then have (aj​,bj​)=(0,1), or its top cell would be an equilibrium. Its bottom column-player payoff must be zero, or its bottom cell would be one. Thus a column ((0,1),(1,0))T occurs. The same argument for the bottom row produces ((1,0),(0,1))T. No column can give the column player payoffs (1,1), since a row-player best response within that column would be a pure equilibrium.
Consequently, if neither pure equilibrium is found, mix equally over the two rows and equally over those two special columns. The row player's two expected payoffs are 1/2; every column gives the column player at most 1/2, and the supported columns achieve 1/2. This is a Nash equilibrium. Computing the two row maxima, scanning for pure equilibria and locating the two special columns takes O(n) running time for n columns.

For two firms, customer value two per site and equal splitting of ties, the payoff to a firm at x against one at y is
u(x,y)=⎩⎨⎧​x+y−1,k,2k−x−y+1,​x<y,x=y,x>y.​
(24)
For x<y, counting sites strictly left of the midpoint and assigning half of an equidistant site's value gives x+y−1, whether x+y is even or odd. The other firm receives the remainder, so this is a constant-sum game with total 2k. Changing tie priority can fundamentally change its Nash equilibria, especially when co-location is permitted.

Final entrant payoff in a discrete location game

Discrete location game OurBigBook.com
For k≥3, suppose two distinct occupied sites are ℓ<r, a final firm must choose a different site, customers have value two per site and nearest-firm ties are split equally. A final firm left of both incumbents maximizes its payoff uniquely at ℓ−1, when that site exists, obtaining 2(ℓ−1). To the right it maximizes uniquely at r+1, obtaining 2(k−r). At every available interior site it obtains the same payoff r−ℓ. Thus all best responses are obtained by comparing these three values, omitting regions with no available site and retaining every tied maximizing choice.
More generally, three distinct locations a<b<c give their left, middle and right firms payoffs a+b−1, c−a and 2k−b−c+1. Counting the two midpoint boundaries proves these formulas; the middle firm's demand is the difference between the cumulative demands at the two boundaries. The formulas retain all even/odd midpoint ties automatically.

If a proposed Pareto improvement changes an assignment, its earliest changed participant loses their unique best available object. With ties or allocation externalities, that argument requires additional assumptions.

Pareto efficiency of serial dictatorship with consecutive friends
Words: 191
Room allocation with friendship externalities OurBigBook.com
Suppose each participant has at most one mutual friend, each friendship pair chooses consecutively, room values lie in [0,1] and are distinct for each participant, and each friendship bonus exceeds 1. Then every subgame perfect equilibrium outcome of serial dictatorship is Pareto optimal.
For a friend pair, if any remaining adjacent room pair exists, the leader chooses their uniquely best room having an available neighbor; the follower chooses their uniquely best available neighbor. Adjacency dominates every possible difference in own-room value for both friends. If no adjacent room pair remains, neither friend can obtain a bonus and each chooses their unique best available room. A participant without a friend also chooses their unique best available room.
For the proof, compare a purported Pareto improvement block by block, where a block is a single participant without a friend or one consecutive friendship pair. Earlier fixed blocks leave the same rooms available. A block receiving adjacency cannot lose it in a weak improvement. Its leader must retain the uniquely best eligible room, and its follower must retain the uniquely best neighboring room. Without available adjacency, both rooms are fixed by strict own-room rankings. Mathematical induction fixes every assignment, excluding a strict improvement.

A pure strategy is a definite, complete plan for a player's choices. In a game with one simultaneous choice, it selects one available action with certainty: heads or tails in matching pennies, for example. In a sequential game it specifies an action at every situation where that player could be called upon to move, including situations never reached when the plan is followed. The plan can use only information available to the player: indistinguishable decision situations must prescribe the same action. An action at one such situation is only part of the plan.
If Si​ is player i's set of pure strategies, the payoff ui​(si​,s−i​) depends on the whole strategy profile. Thus the same pure strategy can be a best response against one opposing choice and perform poorly against another. A dominant strategy is the stronger case in which it is a best response against every opposing strategy profile.

Matching pennies

Words: 336
Bimatrix game OurBigBook.com
Both players choose heads H or tails T without seeing the other's choice. The row player receives 1 when the choices match and −1 when they differ; the column player receives the opposite payoff. Thus matching pennies is a zero-sum game, with ordered payoff pairs:
Row choice / column choiceHT
H(1,−1)(−1,1)
T(−1,1)(1,−1)
At (H,H) the column player improves by switching to T; at (H,T) the row player improves by switching to T; at (T,H) the row player improves by switching to H; at (T,T) the column player improves by switching to H. Every pure strategy strategy profile therefore has a profitable unilateral deviation, so none is a Nash equilibrium.
Let p be the row player's probability of heads and q the column player's probability of heads. Their random choices are independent. Against fixed q, the row player's pure-choice expected payoffs are
U1​(H,q)=2q−1,U1​(T,q)=1−2q.
(27)
Against fixed p, the column player's pure-choice expected payoffs are
U2​(p,H)=1−2p,U2​(p,T)=2p−1.
(28)
Consequently the best responses, expressed as allowed heads probabilities, are
BR1​(q)=⎩⎨⎧​{0}[0,1]{1}​q<1/2,q=1/2,q>1/2,​BR2​(p)=⎩⎨⎧​{1}[0,1]{0}​p<1/2,p=1/2,p>1/2.​
(29)
Here [0,1] means every mixture is a best response, including both pure strategies. If q>1/2, the row player must choose p=1, which makes the column player's best response q=0, a contradiction. If q<1/2, the row player must choose p=0, which forces q=1, also a contradiction. Hence q=1/2; for the column player to mix at this q, the two column payoffs must tie, forcing p=1/2. The unique Nash equilibrium is therefore
p∗=q∗=21​,U1​(p∗,q∗)=U2​(p∗,q∗)=0.
(30)
Indeed, for any p,q, U1​(p,q)=(2p−1)(2q−1) and U2​(p,q)=−U1​(p,q). Holding q=1/2 gives the row player zero for every deviation p′; holding p=1/2 gives the column player zero for every deviation q′. A player is indifferent against the equilibrium mixture, but choosing an arbitrary best response to it need not preserve the opponent's best response. This is why that indifference does not produce additional Nash equilibria.

A(3,2)(0,0)

Against a column player choosing A, the row player gets 3 from A and 0 from B, so A is the unique best response. Against B, the row player gets 0 from A and 2 from B, so B is the unique best response. The column player likewise prefers to match the row choice. Thus (A,A) and (B,B) are pure strategy Nash equilibria, while each mismatched strategy profile has a profitable unilateral deviation.

Notice whose equation determines whose probability: the row player's indifference fixes the column player's q, and the column player's indifference fixes the row player's p.

Pr(A,A)=256​,Pr(A,B)=259​,Pr(B,A)=254​,Pr(B,B)=256​.

Thus they meet with probability 12/25, and each receives expected payoff 3(6/25)+2(6/25)=6/5. Both coordinated pure strategy outcomes strictly improve both players' expected payoffs over (6/5,6/5): (3,2) and (2,3) each do so. The mixed Nash equilibrium therefore fails Pareto efficiency, even though no unilateral deviation helps. Switching together can help when switching alone cannot. Neither coordinated outcome improves both players over the other, and both are Pareto efficient, even when a lottery over joint action profiles is allowed: any positive weight on another outcome reduces the payoff of the player receiving 3.

Nash equilibrium (σ∗)

Words: 1k Articles: 15
Bimatrix game OurBigBook.com
A Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile in which every player's strategy is a best response to the others. For a finite game and mixed strategies, its precise condition is
Ui​(σi∗​,σ−i∗​)≥Ui​(τi​,σ−i∗​)for every player i and every τi​∈Δ(Si​).
(34)
The opponents' strategies σ−i∗​ are held fixed while testing each unilateral deviation. Equality is allowed: a player may have other equally good best responses. Because expected payoff is a linear function of the player's own mixture, it suffices to test every pure strategy. Equivalently, every choice in the support of a mixed strategy must attain the largest pure-choice expected payoff, and no unused choice may exceed it.
The two worked examples illustrate different uses of this condition. Matching pennies has no pure strategy Nash equilibrium, but its unique mixed strategy Nash equilibrium removes each player's vulnerability to predictable play. The asymmetric coordination example has three Nash equilibria, and its mixed one fails Pareto efficiency. A Nash equilibrium tests individual incentives, whereas Pareto efficiency compares feasible outcomes that may require several players to change together. In the prisoner's dilemma, for example, mutual defection is a Nash equilibrium even though mutual cooperation gives both players a larger payoff because R>P.
Existence in a finite game is guaranteed by Nash's theorem. The theorem does not select one Nash equilibrium, promise Pareto efficiency, or assert convergence of a learning process. Nash's [ref] used the Kakutani fixed-point theorem; his [ref] gave a proof using the Brouwer fixed-point theorem. The connection to a fixed point captures the idea of choices that remain mutually optimal when considered together.
