Existential equilibrium checking in a Boolean game

Words: 124
Nash equilibrium OurBigBook.com
Given a Boolean game and a query propositional formula ϕ, decide whether some pure strategy Nash equilibrium satisfies ϕ. The problem is complete for the existential second level of the polynomial hierarchy.
For membership, existentially choose a Boolean valuation and universally check every player's every unilateral deviation. The goal must remain false under all such deviations for each player whose goal is currently false. Each individual check takes polynomial time.
For hardness, start with a two-block quantified Boolean formula ∃X∀Yψ(X,Y). Give player 1 control of X and the constant true goal. Give player 2 control of Y and goal ¬ψ, and use ψ as the query. A queried Nash equilibrium exists exactly when some choice of X leaves player 2 unable to falsify ψ by changing Y. This is precisely the input quantified statement, and the construction is a polynomial-time reduction.

Ranked university application game

Words: 100
Nash equilibrium OurBigBook.com
There are mq distinctly ranked students and m labelled universities with q seats each. Each student applies to one university; each university selects the greatest ranks, and admitted students receive their admitted cohort's average rank. At a pure Nash equilibrium, every student is admitted: any rejected student could move to a university with a vacancy. The university with the largest average must contain the top q ranks, since any omitted higher rank could displace its lowest rank and improve. Repeat on the remaining students to obtain consecutive rank blocks. Assigning these blocks to the labelled universities gives exactly m! pure equilibria.

Symmetric Nash equilibrium

Words: 67
Nash equilibrium OurBigBook.com
In a game invariant under permuting players, a symmetric Nash equilibrium gives every player the same strategy, which may be a mixed strategy. Independent randomization does not require realized resource loads to be equal. When resource delays are affine, a player's expected delay depends on their own certain resource use plus the expected use by the other players; replacing all loads by unconditional total expected loads loses that own-player correction.

Equilibrium oddness theorem

Words: 68
Nash equilibrium OurBigBook.com
A finite nondegenerate bimatrix game has a finite odd number of Nash equilibria. After shifting to positive payoffs, fully labelled vertex pairs in the bounded best-response polytopes correspond to equilibria plus one artificial zero pair. Dropping a fixed label gives a finite path graph whose endpoints are exactly these pairs. The number of endpoints is even, leaving an odd number of genuine equilibria. This is the endpoint-parity argument underlying the Lemke-Howson algorithm.

Symmetric equilibrium

Words: 173 Articles: 3
Nash equilibrium OurBigBook.com
A symmetric equilibrium of a symmetric game has every player use the same strategy or the same distribution of strategies. Symmetry between players does not require identical behavior across contests with different prizes.
Symmetric equilibrium parity
Words: 33
Symmetric equilibrium OurBigBook.com
In a nondegenerate symmetric bimatrix game, player interchange pairs every nonsymmetric Nash equilibrium with a distinct swapped equilibrium. The equilibrium oddness theorem gives an odd total; the remaining fixed points, which are the symmetric equilibria, therefore also number an odd amount.
Symmetric Nash gain map (Ti​(x)=1+∑j​[(Px)j​−xTPx]+​xi​+[(Px)i​−xTPx]+​​)
Words: 107 Articles: 1
Symmetric equilibrium OurBigBook.com
The continuous gain map takes a probability simplex to itself. The Brouwer fixed-point theorem supplies a fixed point, whose positive gains would contradict the zero strategy-weighted average payoff excess. Thus all gains vanish, giving a strategy that is a best response to itself. In a symmetric bimatrix game, this produces a symmetric equilibrium.
Gain-map proof of symmetric equilibrium (Fi​(p)=1+∑j​[e(j,p)−e(p)]+​pi​+[e(i,p)−e(p)]+​​)
Words: 64
Symmetric Nash gain map OurBigBook.com
For a symmetric finite game, pure-action expected payoffs e(i,p) against independent identical opposing mixed strategies are continuous. The displayed map takes the probability simplex continuously into itself. At a Brouwer fixed-point theorem fixed point, put ri​=[e(i,p)−e(p)]+​ and S=∑i​ri​. The fixed-point equations give ri​=pi​S. If S>0, every supported action has strictly positive excess payoff, contradicting ∑i​pi​(e(i,p)−e(p))=0. Hence S=0 and every supported action is a best response, proving a symmetric Nash equilibrium.

Complementarity construction of a symmetric Nash equilibrium (Px+z=1,x,z≥0,xTz=0)

Words: 43
Nash equilibrium OurBigBook.com
For a symmetric bimatrix game with payoff matrices P,PT, any nonzero x satisfying these equations gives the symmetric Nash equilibrium (x/∑i​xi​,x/∑i​xi​). Every positive coordinate attains the same maximal payoff. This one-vector construction differs from a two-vector Lemke-Howson algorithm path, which can return asymmetric equilibria.

Lemke-Howson algorithm

Words: 104 Articles: 1
Nash equilibrium OurBigBook.com
The Lemke-Howson algorithm follows an almost completely labeled path in the product of two best-response polytopes of a bimatrix game. Drop one label at the artificial zero pair, then alternately pivot away the duplicated label until the dropped label returns. A nonzero completely labeled endpoint, after normalization, gives a Nash equilibrium. The two players' vectors must be kept separate even in a symmetric game.
Complementary pivoting (xi​ri​=0,yj​sj​=0)
Words: 42
Lemke-Howson algorithm OurBigBook.com
Complementary pivoting follows adjacent bases while maintaining all but one label of a complementarity system. The Lemke-Howson algorithm for a bimatrix game follows the duplicated label between two tableaux until it restores the dropped label at a nonzero completely labelled pair. Normalization then gives a Nash equilibrium.

Nash's theorem

Words: 83 Articles: 1
Nash equilibrium OurBigBook.com
Nash's theorem states that every finite game has at least one Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies.
Brouwer gain-map proof of bimatrix equilibrium (Ti​(p,q)=1+∑j​[(Aq)j​−pTAq]+​pi​+[(Aq)i​−pTAq]+​​)
Words: 72
Nash's theorem OurBigBook.com
For each player in a finite bimatrix game, add the positive pure-strategy gains to its current mixed strategy and normalize. This gives a continuous self-map of the product of probability simplices. At a Brouwer fixed-point theorem fixed point, the gain coordinates equal the current strategy times their total gain. If that total were positive, every supported action would beat the current average payoff, contradicting that average. Thus every pure deviation has nonpositive gain for both players, proving a Nash equilibrium.

Brouwer proof of Nash equilibrium for a two-by-two game

Words: 33
Nash equilibrium OurBigBook.com
Normalize each player's positive pure-strategy payoff improvements to define a continuous self-map of the product of their mixed-strategy simplices. At a Brouwer fixed point every positive improvement must vanish, giving a Nash equilibrium.

Best response (BRi​(σ−i​))

Words: 259 Articles: 4
Game theory OurBigBook.com
A best response maximizes a player's expected payoff while the other players' strategies are held fixed. In a finite game, write the full set of mixed strategy best responses as
BRi​(σ−i​)={τi​∈Δ(Si​):Ui​(τi​,σ−i​)=maxρi​∈Δ(Si​)​Ui​(ρi​,σ−i​)}.
(35)
This is generally a set-valued mapping, since several choices may tie. Every mixture supported on maximizing pure strategies is a best response, and mixing in a strictly worse choice reduces expected payoff.
For example, against q=3/4 in matching pennies, the row player's heads and tails expected payoffs are 1/2 and −1/2, so heads is the unique best response. Against q=1/2, all mixtures are best responses. In the asymmetric coordination example, against q=3/4 the row player gets 9/4 from A and 1/2 from B, so A is optimal. A Nash equilibrium requires everyone to be a best response simultaneously; one optimal reply alone does not establish it.

Dominant strategy

Words: 143 Articles: 3
Best response OurBigBook.com
A dominant strategy is a best response for every strategy profile of the other players.

Weakly dominant strategy

Words: 51
Dominant strategy OurBigBook.com
A strategy giving at least as large a payoff as every alternative against every opponent strategy profile. Under the convention distinguishing weak dominance from complete payoff equivalence, require a strict advantage somewhere. In a two-action finite game, it suffices to check the opponent's pure strategies: expected payoff differences against an opponent's mixed strategy are weighted averages of those pure-action comparisons.

Dominant-strategy equilibrium (si​∈⋂s−i​​BRi​(s−i​)∀i)

Words: 58
Dominant strategy OurBigBook.com
A strategy profile in which each player uses a dominant strategy. Every such profile is a Nash equilibrium, since each prescribed choice is a best response to the actual opposing choices in particular. The converse fails: a Nash equilibrium only requires a best response to those actual choices. With the weak convention for dominant strategy, ties are allowed; a strictly dominant strategy requires strict improvement over every alternative against every opposing profile.

Strictly dominant strategy

Words: 21
Dominant strategy OurBigBook.com
A strictly dominant strategy gives a strictly greater payoff than every alternative strategy for every strategy profile of the other players.

Zero-sum game (∑i​ui​(s)=0)

Words: 966 Articles: 16
Game theory OurBigBook.com
In a zero-sum game, the players' payoffs sum to zero at every pure strategy strategy profile. For two players this means u2​=−u1​: maximizing the column player's payoff is minimizing the row player's. A single payoff matrix A therefore specifies a finite two-player matrix game, and independent mixed strategies x,y give expected payoffs xTAy and −xTAy.
Matching pennies and the usual rock paper scissors are two-player zero-sum games. The asymmetric coordination example is not: its total payoff is 5 when choices match and 0 otherwise. Applying a two-player minimax theorem to general bimatrix games would discard this possibility of shared gains. For a two-player zero-sum game, however, optimal mixed strategies guarantee the value of a zero-sum game, and pairing any two opposing optimal strategies gives a Nash equilibrium.

Constant-sum game (u1​+u2​=K)

Words: 58
Zero-sum game OurBigBook.com
In a two-player constant-sum game, the sum of the two payoffs is the same constant K at every strategy profile. Replacing each player's payoff by ui​−K/2 gives a zero-sum game without changing best responses or Nash equilibria. If both players can guarantee K/2, then any Nash equilibrium gives each that value. An equilibrium in pure strategies must use pure strategies with that guarantee: otherwise the opponent could improve on K/2 by a unilateral deviation.

Rock paper scissors

Words: 60
Zero-sum game OurBigBook.com
With choices ordered rock, scissors, paper and winner payoff 1, the row-player payoff matrix is (0−11​10−1​−110​). Both the row and column sums vanish. Thus the uniform mixed strategy guarantees expected payoff zero against every opposing strategy; the value of a zero-sum game is zero. A player responding to a known nonuniform mixture can instead optimize its linear expected payoff over pure responses and their ties.

Value of a zero-sum game (v=maxr​mins​rTAs=mins​maxr​rTAs)

Words: 73
Zero-sum game OurBigBook.com
For a finite matrix zero-sum game, the value is the payoff that the maximizing player can guarantee and the minimizing player can prevent the payoff from exceeding, using mixed strategies. The common value of the two displayed optimizations exists by the minimax theorem. A pair of strategies can be verified directly by checking that every pure column pays the row mixture at least v and every pure row earns at most v against the column mixture.

Cost-weighted finite search game (v=(c2+∑i​ci2​)/(2c))

Words: 54
Zero-sum game OurBigBook.com
In a hide-and-search zero-sum game with positive inspection costs ci​ and c=∑i​ci​, hiding with probabilities ci​/c gives the same expected search cost for every complete search order. For three locations, beginning at i with probability ci​/c and randomizing the remaining two orders also equalizes every hiding location. The common value is the displayed quantity.

Matrix game

Zero-sum game OurBigBook.com
A matrix game is a finite two-player zero-sum game whose entry Aij​ is the row player's payoff when the players choose row i and column j.

Positive-payoff linear programming for a matrix game (min1Tx: BTx≥1, x≥0)

Words: 74
Matrix game OurBigBook.com
When every entry of a payoff matrix B is positive, its game value v is positive. Setting x=p/v converts the row player's probability vector and guaranteed value into the displayed linear program, whose optimum is 1/v. Conversely normalizing a feasible x gives a mixed strategy guaranteeing 1/(1Tx). The dual maximizes 1Ty under By≤1, y≥0 and recovers the column strategy by normalization. Adding a constant to every payoff preserves Nash equilibria and lets this positive-payoff formulation handle general finite zero-sum games.

A payoff matrix records the row player's gains when row i meets column j. In a zero-sum game the other player's payoff is the negative. For mixed strategies p,q, the expected row payoff is pTAq.

Minimax theorem (maxx​miny​xTAy=miny​maxx​xTAy)

Words: 205
Zero-sum game OurBigBook.com
For every real m×n payoff matrix A of a two-player zero-sum game, the minimax theorem states
maxx∈Δm​​miny∈Δn​​xTAy=miny∈Δn​​maxx∈Δm​​xTAy=v,
(39)
where Δm​,Δn​ are the players' probability simplices. Both outer optima are attained. The row player's security level payoff is the largest payoff it can guarantee against all opposing choices; the column player can hold that payoff to the same number v, the value of a zero-sum game. For optimal x∗,y∗,
xTAy∗≤v=(x∗)TAy∗≤(x∗)TAyfor all x∈Δm​, y∈Δn​.
(40)
These are exactly the Nash equilibrium inequalities under the row-maximizes, column-minimizes convention. Conversely, a Nash equilibrium of this two-player zero-sum game supplies both guarantees. This equality explains why independent worst-case optimization solves the opposing incentives in this special class.
Allowing mixed strategies is essential. For matching pennies, A=(1−1​−11​). Restricting both players to pure strategies gives maxi​minj​Aij​=−1 and minj​maxi​Aij​=1. Allowing mixed strategies closes the gap: each fair mixture guarantees zero, so v=0. These guarantees hold even if the opponent knows the mixture's probabilities, provided the opponent does not observe the sampled choice before choosing.
John von Neumann proved the two-player zero-sum game result in Zur Theorie der Gesellschaftsspiele, Mathematische Annalen 100, 295–320 (1928); the original article's footnote 7 explicitly discusses the equality of max–min and min–max. Nash's [ref] states that existence of a Nash equilibrium is equivalent to this result in the two-player zero-sum game case, and extends existence to all finite games.

Support certificate for an antisymmetric matrix game (Ap≤0,p≥0,1Tp=1)

Antisymmetric zero-sum game OurBigBook.com
For an antisymmetric payoff matrix, such a vector guarantees that an opponent playing rows cannot win positively against it. Antisymmetry also gives pTA≥0, so the same mixed strategy guarantees nonnegative payoff as a row strategy and proves game value zero. Furthermore pTAp=0 forces (Ap)i​=0 whenever pi​>0. To prove uniqueness, use one certified strategy q: any other optimal p satisfies qTAp=−(Aq)Tp, so a strict negative component of Aq forces the corresponding probability in p to vanish.

Consecutive-number antisymmetric game

Words: 91
Antisymmetric zero-sum game OurBigBook.com
In this game the higher of two chosen integers wins one unit if they are consecutive, but pays two units if their difference is at least two. Ties pay zero. For any choices 1,…,n with n≥3, both players can optimally choose 1,2,3 with probabilities 1/4,1/2,1/4 and assign zero probability to larger numbers. If p is this vector, Ap is zero in its first three entries, −5/4 in its fourth when present, and −2 in all later entries. Thus Ap≤0 and pTA≥0, proving the zero value and both security guarantees.

Dominated strategy

Words: 406 Articles: 5
Game theory OurBigBook.com
A dominated strategy can be replaced by another strategy that performs at least as well against every opponent action.

Very weakly dominated strategy (ui​(si​,s−i​)≤ui​(σi​,s−i​) for every s−i​)

Words: 137
Dominated strategy OurBigBook.com
A pure strategy is very weakly dominated by another strategy when its payoff is no greater against every opposing pure strategy profile, with no strict advantage required anywhere. The definition permits payoff-equivalent strategies and even domination by the original strategy itself. A weakly dominated strategy instead has a strict inequality for at least one opposing strategy profile.
In a binary game, suppose σi​ very weakly dominates si​ and assigns positive probability to a different pure action. At every opposing strategy profile where si​ pays one, all actions in the support of a mixed strategy must also pay one. Where si​ pays zero, their payoffs are automatically no smaller. Therefore every distinct supported action very weakly dominates si​. If the mixed domination is weak with a strict improvement somewhere, choose a supported action paying one at a profile where si​ pays zero; that action also supplies a strict improvement. The requirement of nontrivial support is indispensable for the very-weak version.

Dominated strategy elimination

Words: 47
Dominated strategy OurBigBook.com
In a finite zero-sum game, removing a strictly dominated strategy preserves the value of a zero-sum game: replace any probability on it by the dominating pure strategy. This increases every payoff for the maximizing player, or decreases every payoff for the minimizing player. Repeat on the reduced game; new domination relations may appear after a deletion.

Weakly dominated strategy

Words: 203 Articles: 2
Dominated strategy OurBigBook.com
A strategy is weakly dominated if another gives at least as much payoff against every opponent strategy and strictly more against at least one. Unlike a strictly dominated strategy, it may remain a best response to opponents who never choose a strategy where the comparison is strict. Thus weak domination does not exclude equilibrium strategies.

Equilibrium preservation under iterated weak dominance

Words: 104
Weakly dominated strategy OurBigBook.com
Starting from the full finite bimatrix game, sequentially remove actions weakly dominated by current mixed strategies, with a strict improvement somewhere. At least one Nash equilibrium survives on the final action sets. Take an Nash equilibrium of the reduced game and restore actions in reverse. A restored action is no better against the fixed surviving opponent strategy than its dominating mixture of already available actions, so it introduces no profitable deviation. Any self-weight in a dominating mixture can be removed and renormalized because strict improvement forces that weight below one. Using dominance tested only against an arbitrary initially restricted opponent set does not guarantee an Nash equilibrium of the original full game.

Weak domination does not exclude equilibrium strategies

Words: 54
Weakly dominated strategy OurBigBook.com
In the zero-sum game with row payoff matrix (00​10​), the second row is weakly dominated by the first. Nevertheless second row and first column form a Nash equilibrium: both rows tie against that column, and both columns tie against that row. Weak dominance therefore cannot be used to discard all possible equilibrium strategies without further qualifications.
